extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners working on health/medical misinformation detection, fact-checking, and mitigation (computer scientists, information scientists, public-health policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for building, annotating, and assessing datasets, fact‑checking tools, detection models, and mitigation strategies for health misinformation in social networks; includes desiderata for datasets, tool rating schemes, and mitigation properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset modality coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets should include multiple data modalities and sources (e.g., news articles, social platform posts, tweets, user engagements, news releases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the survey: datasets including 5,216 news, 296,752 related user engagements, and 958 social platform posts; multimodal repositories with articles and Twitter posts. Datasets intended as benchmarks should gather rich data from social media and the Web to support content‑, propagation‑, and source‑based methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground truth and evidence annotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in datasets should be paired with ground truth labels and, where possible, with supporting/refuting evidence documents and evidence sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: COVID-Fact contains 4,086 claims with corresponding evidence documents and evidence sentences. Recommendation: annotate evidence to support/refute claims so models can learn verifiable justification, not just labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation method (manual vs automatic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets must document whether labels were produced manually (experts or crowd-sourced) or automatically (heuristics, keyword labeling), since annotation method affects quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many collected datasets use manual expert annotation; others use automatic filtering for true/refuted claims or keyword/hashtag labeling (e.g., pro‑/anti‑vaccine labeled using hashtags). Report annotation provenance and inter-annotator procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation expertise and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotations for medical misinformation should ideally be done by domain experts and include expert-based manual fact-checking services for label reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey recommends that dataset annotation be done by experts and that authoritative expert-based manual fact-checking services be incorporated. Where non-expert annotation is used, document limitations and validation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation granularity and rating scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets and fact-checking resources should specify rating scales or label taxonomies (binary/ multiclass/graded) and provide clear definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: HealthNewsReview.org rates news stories/releases on 10 criteria with ratings from 0 to 5; Snopes uses labels like True, Mostly True, Mixture, Mostly False, Unproven; Washington Post uses 0–4 pinocchios. Specify whether labels are binary, multiclass, or continuous/graded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical breadth (medical topics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benchmark datasets should cover a broad range of medical topics beyond a single crisis (e.g., beyond COVID-19 to smoking, drugs, diets, self‑treatment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey calls for datasets covering diverse medical topics to avoid overfitting to a single event and to support generalizable detection/mitigation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal coverage and uncertainty handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets and evaluation must account for temporality and medical uncertainty (scientific knowledge evolves; facts may be probabilistic or change over time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design annotation schemas and model evaluation that reflect uncertainty, provide timestamps, and allow reclassification as knowledge changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilingual and cross-platform support
rubrics_metrics.description: Datasets should include multi-language and multi-platform content to reflect real-world misinformation ecosystems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the survey: 16K tweets annotated in four languages; multi-language/multimodal news and Twitter posts. Benchmarks should include languages and platform types to support robust methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset suitability for detection paradigms
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference dataset should satisfy requirements of content-based, propagation-based, and source-based misinformation detection methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That means including textual content, propagation/network traces, and source metadata (user profiles, credibility signals) so different detection approaches can be fairly compared.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking tool attributes to report
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing or evaluating fact‑checking tools, report whether they are manual or automatic, available APIs, themes covered, and their rating scale for credibility assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 8 shows examples: Snopes (Manual; covers politics, health; rating scale like True/Mostly True/etc.), Google Fact Check (API/markup + explorer), PolitiFact (manual with scorecards). Evaluations should document these tool attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-check selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedures for choosing claims to check should be explicit; common heuristics include verifiability and likelihood of being propagated by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PolitiFact considers questions like 'Is the statement rooted in a fact that is verifiable?' and 'Is the statement likely to be passed on and repeated by others?'. Use similar explicit criteria when sampling claims for fact‑checking datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-checking review process rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact-checking processes should be transparent about review stages (e.g., multi-stage review, involvement of external academics) and whether they combine manual and automatic steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full Fact uses a three-stage review that may involve external academics and is moving toward hybrid manual/automatic methods; such procedural transparency aids trust and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation desiderata: transparency, explainability, fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigation approaches should provide transparency, explainability, and fairness guarantees to build trust among producers, consumers, and gatekeepers of information flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey explicitly advocates these properties for mitigation systems; evaluations should include measures of explainability and fairness and report any trade-offs with effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-centric mitigation: leveraging user roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigation methods should leverage user roles (opinion leaders, correctors/guardians) — identify influential spreaders and empower correctors with tools (e.g., fact‑checking URL recommendation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: detecting guardians who attach fact‑checking URLs and designing recommendation models to motivate them; target opinion leaders for interventions to maximize impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source-based mitigation: detect and remove malicious accounts/bots
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques should identify malicious sources (bots, fake users) and remove or restrict them to reduce misinformation spread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bot detection methods look for repeated posting of similar content or bot‑like engagement patterns; once detected, platforms can remove or limit accounts. Report detection precision/recall and downstream impact of removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network-structure interventions and immunization
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions can act on network structure: block propagation paths, identify smallest/high-impact sets of nodes to immunize/decontaminate, or use competing-cascade seeding to promote true news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include IC and LT diffusion models, greedy selection, centrality heuristics, dynamic blocking strategies, decontamination that targets contaminated users until a desired fraction is reached, and competing cascades to maximize true-news influence while minimizing fake-news spread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community detection and targeted blocking
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect and monitor communities where fake news is frequent and apply dynamic blocking or tailored interventions at the community level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey highlights measuring influence within communities and employing algorithms with dynamic blocking strategies to minimize rumor impact; evaluations should measure community-level spread reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of true news as mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigation may include promoting reliable information by targeting users exposed to false news or selecting trusted seeds to propagate true news in competition with false news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competing Cascades and decontamination methods are examples; effectiveness depends on seed selection, trusted sources, and timing; evaluate via simulated or real diffusion outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid modeling: combine statistical learning with symbolic knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Detection systems should incorporate authoritative ground-truth knowledge and symbolic logic (knowledge bases, reasoning rules) alongside machine learning for robustness in the medical domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey recommends hybrid approaches that fuse deep learning representation with strict logic reasoning to enforce constraints and exploit validated domain knowledge; evaluate hybrid models on explainability and robustness to adversarial imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation benchmark and comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers should aim to create and use common reference datasets and standardized evaluation protocols to enable fair comparison across methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey finds many custom datasets hinder comparison; calls for collaborative creation of reference datasets annotated by experts, covering multiple modalities and topics, and including content/propagation/source signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adversarial robustness and evolving threat models
rubrics_metrics.description: Detection and mitigation methods should be evaluated against evolving adversarial tactics (e.g., LLM‑generated text, bots mimicking human propagation), since fake-news producers adapt to mimic valid news and propagation patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design adversarial evaluation scenarios and measure degradation as adversaries become more sophisticated; consider defenses that do not rely solely on static stylistic features.
